title: Broad, fast, regular — and the patient is talking
presentingComplaint: Sudden onset of rapid palpitations twenty minutes ago with chest discomfort and light-headedness.
history: Anterior myocardial infarction four years ago with impaired left ventricular function
On aspirin, bisoprolol, ramipril and atorvastatin
Two previous episodes of similar palpitations, one requiring hospital treatment
symptoms: Rapid, regular pounding in the chest
examinationFindings: Pale, alert and talking in short sentences
Regular fast pulse of small volume; cool peripheries
Jugular venous pressure raised with intermittent cannon a waves
Variable intensity of the first heart sound

vitals.bedside: Conscious, talking, but pale with a systolic pressure in the nineties. A broad-complex tachycardia in a patient with a previous infarct is ventricular tachycardia until proved otherwise.

ecg.pWaves: No P waves are related to the QRS complexes. Occasional dissociated P waves can be found marching through at a slower, independent rate
ecg.prInterval: Not applicable — there is atrioventricular dissociation
ecg.qrs: 0.17 s, broad and monomorphic, with a slurred upstroke and no discrete Q, R and S components
ecg.axis: Extreme, with concordance across the precordial leads
ecg.stSegment: Discordant depression, secondary to abnormal ventricular activation
keyFindings: A regular, broad-complex tachycardia at 176 bpm
Atrioventricular dissociation — independent P waves, cannon a waves and variable S1 at the bedside
Very broad QRS (0.17 s) with a slurred upstroke and precordial concordance
A history of previous myocardial infarction, which alone makes ventricular tachycardia far more likely than any alternative

interpretation: Regular monomorphic broad-complex tachycardia at 176 bpm with evidence of atrioventricular dissociation — findings consistent with ventricular tachycardia. In a patient with previous myocardial infarction, a broad-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia unless proved otherwise.

auscultation.note: The intensity of the first heart sound varies from beat to beat, because the dissociated atria contract at a different phase of each ventricular cycle. This is an audible sign of atrioventricular dissociation.
Look at the neck while you listen: intermittent cannon a waves are produced when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.

options.text: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: Correct. A regular broad-complex tachycardia with atrioventricular dissociation in a patient with previous infarction.

options.text: Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction
options.feedback: Possible in principle, but far less likely: dissociated P waves, a QRS of 0.17 s, precordial concordance and a history of infarction all point to ventricular origin.

options.text: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block and bundle branch block
options.feedback: That would give a rate near 150 with identifiable flutter waves, and the QRS would carry a recognisable bundle branch morphology.

options.text: Ventricular fibrillation
options.feedback: Ventricular fibrillation has no organised complexes at all and no cardiac output. This patient is conscious with a pulse.

questions.explanation: The safest rule in medicine's most dangerous tracing: a broad-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proved otherwise, particularly with a history of structural heart disease.

questions.prompt: Which finding most strongly confirms a ventricular origin?

options.text: Atrioventricular dissociation, with capture or fusion beats if present
options.feedback: Correct. Dissociation, capture beats and fusion beats are effectively diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia, though they are seen in only a minority of tracings.

options.text: A rate above 150 bpm
options.feedback: Rate does not distinguish ventricular from supraventricular tachycardia.

options.text: The presence of chest discomfort
options.feedback: Symptoms reflect haemodynamics, not the origin of the rhythm. A well-tolerated broad-complex tachycardia is still very often ventricular.

options.text: A normal blood pressure
options.feedback: A dangerous misconception: many patients maintain their blood pressure in ventricular tachycardia for a considerable time.

questions.explanation: Haemodynamic stability tells you how urgent the situation is. It tells you nothing about where the rhythm comes from.

questions.prompt: Which QRS features favour a ventricular origin?

options.text: Very broad complexes (> 0.16 s), a slurred upstroke, extreme axis and precordial concordance
options.feedback: Correct. These features are all incorporated into the published diagnostic algorithms for broad-complex tachycardia.

options.text: A QRS of exactly 0.12 s with a typical bundle branch morphology
options.feedback: A typical bundle branch pattern at the lower end of the broad range would favour a supraventricular rhythm with aberrancy.

options.text: A short PR interval with a delta wave
options.feedback: That is pre-excitation, which is a different mechanism of broad-complex tachycardia and matters because nodal blocking drugs can be dangerous.

options.text: Peaked T waves
options.feedback: That suggests hyperkalaemia, which can produce a broad complex rhythm but with a different overall appearance.

questions.explanation: Precordial concordance — all precordial QRS complexes pointing the same way — is a specific sign, because no bundle branch pattern produces it.

questions.prompt: Given the previous infarct and this tracing, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: Correct. Surviving myocyte bundles within and around an old infarct scar create the slow-conduction zone that sustains a re-entrant circuit.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia with pre-existing bundle branch block
options.feedback: Sinus tachycardia would have P waves related to every QRS at a constant interval.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction over an accessory pathway
options.feedback: That produces an irregular, bizarre, often very fast broad-complex tachycardia. This rhythm is regular and monomorphic.

options.text: Artefact from patient movement
options.feedback: Artefact is a genuine cause of pseudo-ventricular-tachycardia, but it is usually recognisable by underlying complexes marching through — and the patient here is symptomatic with a matching pulse.

questions.explanation: Previous myocardial infarction is the single strongest predictor of ventricular origin in a broad-complex tachycardia — stronger than any ECG criterion.

questions.prompt: He is conscious with a systolic pressure of 92 mmHg and chest discomfort. Which principle applies in this educational scenario?

options.text: Treat as ventricular tachycardia, involve senior help immediately, and prepare for synchronised cardioversion if adverse features are present
options.feedback: Correct. Chest pain, hypotension, syncope or heart failure are the adverse features that indicate immediate synchronised cardioversion under sedation.

options.text: Give verapamil, since the rhythm is probably supraventricular
options.feedback: This is one of the most dangerous errors in acute cardiology. Verapamil in ventricular tachycardia can cause haemodynamic collapse.

options.text: Observe for two hours to see whether it terminates spontaneously
options.feedback: Sustained ventricular tachycardia with adverse features requires immediate treatment.

options.text: Give unsynchronised defibrillation
options.feedback: In a patient with a pulse, cardioversion must be synchronised; an unsynchronised shock risks inducing ventricular fibrillation.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Broad-complex tachycardia is managed under senior supervision following current resuscitation council guidance.

explanation: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia after myocardial infarction is a re-entrant arrhythmia. Islands of surviving myocardium within the infarct scar conduct slowly, creating a circuit around which the impulse can travel indefinitely. Because activation begins in ventricular muscle rather than in the conducting system, it spreads cell to cell — slowly — so the QRS is very broad with a slurred upstroke and no discrete Q, R and S components. The atria continue under sinus control and are unrelated to the ventricles, which produces atrioventricular dissociation on the tracing and, at the bedside, intermittent cannon a waves and a first heart sound that varies in intensity. The clinical rule is unambiguous: a broad-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proved otherwise, and treating it as supraventricular is far more dangerous than the reverse.
learningObjectives: Apply the rule that broad-complex tachycardia is ventricular until proved otherwise
Identify atrioventricular dissociation on the tracing and at the bedside
List the QRS features that favour a ventricular origin
Recognise that haemodynamic stability does not indicate a supraventricular origin
clinicalContext: The surface ECG cannot always be certain of the mechanism. A previous tracing in sinus rhythm, the clinical history and — definitively — electrophysiological study resolve the remaining uncertainty.
